creator: Jacob Rees-Mogg
title: A Bond Market failure would be catastrophic
full_text:
The gilt market really matters. What is
happening is tremendously important and
risks a financial crisis.
I don't want to scare people, but
equally I don't want to mince my words.
Government credit is fundamental to the
stability of the modern nation-state. It
is how the modern nation-state operates.
Because the government never has
sufficient funds from taxation to pay
for its ordinary expenses, it has to go
to the market to get it.
But it goes to the market to get
something that has an ethereal
existence.
We have no underlying value to our
currency. There is an essential element
of it that is purely confidence. If
you're a pessimist, you would say a
confidence trick.
And maintaining that confidence is
essential
to stability.
And the risk
is that when things begin to turn, they
get out of hand very quickly.
It's not to say there aren't warning
signs about a crisis. Those are already
sounding.
But that if they're not acted upon, then
you can go remarkably quickly. Think
back to the financial crisis of 19 of
198 of 2008
from it being a problem of Bear Stearns,
of Lehman Brothers, to a risk to the
whole banking system.
And the same is happening now in this
country. The moment it is a manageable
problem, but if nothing is done, it can
get out of hand.
Why do gilts matter?
Why can't governments just tax a little
bit more or print money?
Well, you can't tax more when interest
rates are rising because you reduce
economic activity further.
You create a downturn in economic
activity because there's less money
around, and this compounds
the reduction in economic activity
caused by high interest rates. High
interest rates deter investment because
they become more expensive, they deter
mortgages being taken out for the same
reason,
and they make people feel poorer because
money that they used to have
after they'd serviced their debt is now
going purely on the service of their
debt. Savers are better off, but
economic growth is dependent on
borrowers, not on savers. So, high
interest rates slow the economy. That's
why they're put up to deal with
inflation.
Um but at the same point, high interest
rates harm households because of the
effect that they have on mortgages and
the reduction of disposable income. So,
if you then increase
income tax or other taxation, you take
even more money away from consumers.
They have left to less to spend,
which adds to the reduction in money
that is available for investment because
of high interest rates. So, you have a
double whammy effect on the economy.
That's why you can't just put taxes up
to deal with it.
Why can't you just print money?
Well, fiat currencies, that is to say
currency that's just printed by
governments, that is not based on
anything, has no intrinsic value.
And if you just print it,
you then create a surfeit of it. This is
what happened in the Weimar Republic and
indeed in Zimbabwe more recently. You
get the point where the money has no
value
and you have runaway inflation.
It's very straightforward monetary
policy that if you print unlimited
money, it has zero value. And so, the
government has to borrow money that is
already in existence rather than
creating new money
to finance its operations if it wishes
to avoid inflation.
You undermine the whole confidence
element of money if you produce
unlimited amounts of it.
So, the bond market matters because it
sets interest rates not just for the
government, but for the investor and for
the mortgage holder.
It's also important as an indicator of
confidence in the solvency of a nation.
Does a nation have its public finances
under control?
Because very few countries now, and this
has been a change in Japan in recent
years, are dependent entirely on
domestic savers. Most of them are now
dependent on foreign flows to fund them.
But the foreigners will not invest if
they do not have confidence
in the underlying economy in which
they're investing in. They expect it to
be able to grow and to repay its debt.
The last time the UK failed to repay its
debt was in 1671-72
with the stop of the Exchequer when
payments were technically only delayed
and that led to significant financial
difficulties
and you could argue through to the
Glorious Revolution.
That's my point about debt markets being
fundamental for the confidence in
governments. The ability of the British
government borrowing the 18th century
was fundamental to our ability to win
the wars against Louis the 14th and
ultimately against in the early 19th
century Napoleon. Why? Because we could
finance them because people trusted
they'd be paid back
and they were getting an interest rate
that was proportionate. But there were
times when interest rates went through
the roof at the point at which people
thought the country was in real trouble.
And that's the risk now that investors
think the country is in real economic
trouble and therefore the government
needs to come up with some answers. It
needs to cut expenditure. I've already
explained why
increasing taxes won't work but you
cannot run an indefinite large deficit
if interest rates are rising because it
will just make them rise further. And
you will find that to attract the next
pound of debt, you have to offer an even
higher interest rate. Therefore, you
need to reduce demand for borrowing and
the way to reduce demand for borrowing
is by cutting expenditure.
And it needs to be done in an orderly
fashion. It is worth remembering that
every single Labour government in the
1930s, in the 1940s, in the 1960s,
in the 1970s,
in the 2000s
has ended with a financial crisis.
Every time a financial crisis has got
them
because they've spent too much and
they've tried to borrow too much from
markets that were not willing to lend to
them.
If they are sensible, they will tackle
it now
rather than pushing it into the long
grass. We are not in a crisis yet, but
we are in the foothills of a crisis. And
when a crisis comes, it comes very
rapidly, very suddenly, and it washes
everything away.
It's not easy to stop once it's started.
You have to be prepared early. Now is
the time to be preparing. The warning
signs are there.
The government should take notice of
this. It really matters. It matters the
whole economy. It is not just a
financing trick. It is central to the
modern state, to our security, to our
ability to run our economy, and to
safeguard our nation.
Watch the gilt market closely. It's not
out of control yet,
but it could be heading in that
direction.
I'm sorry to be so gloomy.

notes.note: The 2008 financial crisis was a banking crisis, not caused by Labour overspending. The UK Treasury's Permanent Secretary called it 'a banking crisis pure and simple', and the independent OBR concluded overspending did not cause the deficit.
notes.claim: United Kingdom Labour governments' financial crises were caused by excessive spending and attempting to borrow too much from markets unwilling to lend.
notes.context_quote: Every time a financial crisis has got them because they've spent too much and they've tried to borrow too much from markets that were not willing to lend to them.
notes.context_paragraph: It is worth remembering that every single Labour government in the 1930s, in the 1940s, in the 1960s, in the 1970s, in the 2000s has ended with a financial crisis. Every time a financial crisis has got them because they've spent too much and they've tried to borrow too much from markets that were not willing to lend to them.

sources.quote: The permanent secretary to the Treasury, Sir Nicholas Macpherson, has argued that the 2008 financial crisis was “a banking crisis pure and simple”, contradicting Conservative claims that it was caused by [Labour](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/labour) overspending.
sources.explanation: Shows the Treasury Permanent Secretary described the 2008 crisis as a banking crisis, contradicting Labour-overspending claims.

sources.quote: The independent [Office for Budget Responsibility](https://www.theguardian.com/business/office-for-budget-responsibility), in its main assessment of the causes of the crisis written in September last year, has taken a more nuanced view. It argues overspending did not cause the deficit or the banking crisis, but that the UK government was less well prepared for the crisis due to a consistently over optimistic view of the revenues the Treasury was likely to receive from 2003 onwards.
sources.explanation: Shows the independent OBR is the source for the claim that overspending did not cause the deficit or banking crisis.

sources.quote: “Looking back to the pre-crisis period, it is hard to argue that the tax and spending policies implemented in the early and mid-2000s were in themselves an important cause of the crisis, or the recession.”
sources.explanation: Direct OBR quote supporting that pre-crisis tax and spending policies were not an important cause of the crisis or recession.

notes.note: The 1945-1951 Attlee Labour government did not end with a financial crisis. Its major financial crises were in 1947 and 1949, by 1950 the balance of payments was in surplus, and it left office after losing the 1951 election despite winning 48.8% of the vote.
notes.claim: The United Kingdom Labour government of the 1930s ended with a financial crisis.
notes.context_quote: It is worth remembering that every single Labour government in the 1930s, in the 1940s, in the 1960s, in the 1970s, in the 2000s has ended with a financial crisis.
notes.context_paragraph: It is worth remembering that every single Labour government in the 1930s, in the 1940s, in the 1960s, in the 1970s, in the 2000s has ended with a financial crisis. Every time a financial crisis has got them because they've spent too much and they've tried to borrow too much from markets that were not willing to lend to them.

sources.quote: The Attlee Labour government of 1945-51 ended more with a whimper than a bang.
sources.explanation: States the government ended without a dramatic financial collapse, unlike 1931.

sources.quote: In contrast to the break-up of the MacDonald Labour government in 1931 there was no ‘bankers’ ramp’ or dramatic and overwhelming financial crisis.
sources.explanation: Directly supports the claim it did not end with a financial crisis.

sources.quote: But from 1947 onwards the government started to run into difficulties and its reputation for competence took a battering as it struggled with economic crises and other problems (notably the fuel crisis and convertibility in 1947, and devaluation in 1949).
sources.explanation: Dates the major economic crises to 1947 and 1949, as claimed in the note.

sources.quote: In 1949, there was another balance of payments crisis, forcing a devaluation of the pound.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim of a 1949 financial crisis.

sources.quote: Britain did benefit from the Marshall Aid plan, improving the economy from 1948, and by 1950 the balance of payments was showing a surplus.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that by 1950 the balance of payments was in surplus.

sources.quote: In October 1951, Britain went to the polls again, this time with the Conservatives winning a majority and Attlee leaving Number 10.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim it left office after losing the 1951 election.

sources.quote: This time, Labour was defeated, despite gaining over 200,000 more votes than Churchill’s Conservatives.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim it lost despite winning more votes.

sources.quote: and when Attlee sought to improve that position in October 1951, Labour lost out to a resurgent Conservative Party which remained in power until 1964.
sources.explanation: Supports the claim it left office after losing the 1951 election.

sources.quote: Its sad fate is even more mysterious because in 1951 Labour’s vote share at 48.8% was almost as high as it was in 1945 and meant the party won nearly a quarter of a million more votes than the victorious Conservatives.
sources.explanation: Supports the 48.8% vote share and winning more votes than the victors.
